text:
PREMISE: Union members earn more than nonunion workers, so unions raise pay.

STEP 1: BLS: union members earned a median $1,404 a week in 2025. Nonunion workers earned $1,174.
STEP 2: A raw gap isn't proof. Union jobs may differ in industry, age or location.
STEP 3: Studies that compare similar workers in similar jobs still find a union pay premium.
STEP 4: That premium is smaller than the raw gap, but it's real.

CONCLUSION: Unions raise pay. Use the honest number, not just the biggest one.

PREMISE: A think tank says raising the minimum wage kills jobs.

STEP 1: First question: who funds it? That tells you whose interests to watch for.
STEP 2: Funding doesn't make an argument wrong. Check the method and the data.
STEP 3: Compare it with other studies and with real results. Nineteen states raised wages on Jan. 1, 2026.
STEP 4: If the claim only holds up when you ignore those results, it's weak.

CONCLUSION: Follow the money, then check the math. Beat the argument, not just the funder.

PREMISE: Politicians say the 2025 budget law helps working families.

STEP 1: Don't argue about the label. Ask who gains and who loses, in dollars.
STEP 2: CBO: the lowest-income 10% of households lose about $1,200 a year on average.
STEP 3: CBO: the top 10% gain about $13,600 a year on average.
STEP 4: For the bottom tenth, that loss is about 3% of income.

CONCLUSION: Who benefits is a question with an answer. Here the scorekeeper gave it.

PREMISE: Louisiana has to choose: good jobs or clean air.

STEP 1: Ask who set up the choice. Usually it's the side that profits from it.
STEP 2: Plant workers breathe the same air as their neighbors.
STEP 3: Coastal restoration has spent about $21.4 billion since 2005. That's jobs that clean up instead of pollute.
STEP 4: Other states run industry under tighter rules. The choice isn't forced by nature.

CONCLUSION: Most 'this or that' choices are false. Demand both, and name who benefits from the trade-off.

PREMISE: My pay went up 4.6% this year, so I'm ahead.

STEP 1: That's the nominal raise. Prices matter too.
STEP 2: BLS: median weekly pay rose 4.6% in spring 2026. Prices rose 3.9%.
STEP 3: Adjusted for prices, real median weekly pay rose about $2 in 1982–84 dollars.
STEP 4: A raise that only covers inflation is standing still.

CONCLUSION: Always ask: real or nominal? Raises are measured in groceries, not digits.

PREMISE: Median income hit a record, so everyone is doing better.

STEP 1: The median is the middle household. It says nothing about the top or bottom.
STEP 2: Census: real median household income was $87,460 in 2025, a record.
STEP 3: Fed: the top 1% held about 31.6% of household wealth. The bottom half held about 2.5%.
STEP 4: The middle can rise while the gap still grows.

CONCLUSION: Good news for the middle and a lopsided top can both be true. Report both.

PREMISE: Work deaths are down nationally, so job safety is fixed.

STEP 1: A national average blends safe and dangerous places together.
STEP 2: The national fatal injury rate was 3.3 per 100,000 in 2024.
STEP 3: Louisiana's was 5.1. Latino work deaths in Louisiana rose from 12 to 22.
STEP 4: The average fell while some groups got worse.

CONCLUSION: Averages hide people. Break the number down before you trust it.

PREMISE: Most poor people in America are white, so poverty isn't about race.

STEP 1: Two different numbers: how many people, and what share of a group.
STEP 2: White Americans are the largest group of poor people by count because they're the largest group.
STEP 3: Black Americans have a higher poverty rate. Census put it at 17.3% in 2025.
STEP 4: Both facts are true. Each one alone misleads.

CONCLUSION: Give the count and the rate. Poverty hits every race, and harder for some. That's why solidarity works.
sources: UC Davis Center for Poverty and Inequality

text:
PREMISE: Louisiana's land loss has slowed, so the problem is shrinking.

STEP 1: Check the time window. Trends depend on where you start and stop.
STEP 2: USGS found loss slowed from 2008 to 2016.
STEP 3: USGS also said the main reason was probably no major hurricane hitting the wetlands in that stretch.
STEP 4: A quiet storm season is luck, not a fix.

CONCLUSION: Ask why a trend changed before you celebrate it.

PREMISE: My cousin saw someone buy steak with SNAP. The program is a scam.

STEP 1: One story isn't a pattern. About 42 million people relied on SNAP in 2024.
STEP 2: Average SNAP benefits work out to roughly $6 a day per person (computed from monthly averages).
STEP 3: CBO's estimated $186 billion in SNAP cuts come mostly from work rules and cost shifts, not fraud.
STEP 4: Even if one purchase bothers you, it doesn't describe millions of families.

CONCLUSION: Anecdotes move feelings. Data shows the pattern. Use the data.

PREMISE: The rich pay most federal income tax, so they pay their fair share.

STEP 1: Share of tax only means something next to share of income.
STEP 2: Top earners get a huge share of income, so they pay a big share of income tax.
STEP 3: Income tax is one tax. Payroll tax stops at $184,500 in wages in 2026.
STEP 4: Sales taxes take a bigger bite from low incomes. In Louisiana, ITEP found the lowest 20% pay a higher share of income in state and local taxes than the top 1%.

CONCLUSION: Look at all taxes, as a share of income. Then judge what's fair.

PREMISE: Black taxpayers get audited more, so the IRS must be racist on purpose.

STEP 1: Separate the effect from the motive.
STEP 2: Treasury-linked research found Black taxpayers were audited at higher rates.
STEP 3: The researchers tied it largely to how audits targeted certain credit claims, not to race data, which the IRS doesn't use.
STEP 4: We can prove the effect. We can't prove anyone's intent.

CONCLUSION: Fight the effect. It's unfair whatever the intent. Don't claim motives you can't show.

PREMISE: Denka gave LaPlace cancer.

STEP 1: Know what's documented. EPA sued in 2023, saying the cancer risk to neighbors was too high.
STEP 2: Elevated risk across a community is not proof that one plant caused one person's illness.
STEP 3: Denka denies its emissions endangered residents. The government dropped the case in 2025.
STEP 4: The documented fact is already serious: federal regulators found the risk unacceptable.

CONCLUSION: Say exactly what the record shows. The truth is strong enough without stretching it.

PREMISE: The USDA stopped the hunger survey to hide hunger.

STEP 1: What we know: USDA ended the survey in 2025.
STEP 2: What we also know: it released a final report in December 2025, showing 47.9 million people in food-insecure households in 2024.
STEP 3: What we don't know: anyone's private motive.
STEP 4: The effect is clear. There will be no count for 2025.

CONCLUSION: Claim the effect: they stopped counting. Leave the mind-reading out.

PREMISE: Louisiana can't afford the $50 billion Coastal Master Plan.

STEP 1: Every cost needs its comparison. What does doing nothing cost?
STEP 2: The plan is about $50 billion over 50 years, roughly $1 billion a year.
STEP 3: The state estimates damage could reach $15 billion a year by 2070 without it.
STEP 4: Paying $1 to avoid up to $15 is cheap.

CONCLUSION: 'Can we afford it?' only makes sense next to 'Can we afford not to?'

PREMISE: Oil companies already paid their taxes. They don't owe the coast anything else.

STEP 1: Some costs never show up on a company's books. Economists call them externalities.
STEP 2: A federal study tied canals and spoil banks to at least 30% to 60% of wetland loss from 1955 to 1978.
STEP 3: That loss now shows up as storm risk, insurance bills and restoration costs.
STEP 4: Taxes on profits don't pay for damage that was never priced.

CONCLUSION: Ask who pays the costs that aren't on the bill.

PREMISE: Nobody complains about industrial tax breaks, so they must be fine.

STEP 1: When a benefit is concentrated and the cost is spread thin, the fight is lopsided.
STEP 2: One company saves millions. Each taxpayer loses a little and may never notice.
STEP 3: So the company hires lobbyists, and the public stays quiet.
STEP 4: Silence is a sign of the setup, not proof of fairness.

CONCLUSION: Small costs spread across millions can add up to billions. Do the addition.
sources: Ohio River Valley Institute, via Louisiana Illuminator (estimate)

text:
PREMISE: Immigrants working for less is their business. It doesn't affect me.

STEP 1: Follow the incentive. If one group can be paid less, bosses can use them to pull everyone down.
STEP 2: BLS: full-time foreign-born workers earned 85.7% of native-born pay in 2025.
STEP 3: A worker who can be deported or is tied to one boss can't push back.
STEP 4: That weak spot sets the floor for the whole shop.

CONCLUSION: Divide workers and every paycheck sinks. Equal rights for all is self-defense.

PREMISE: Some jobs pay well and some don't. That's just skill.

STEP 1: Skill matters. So does bargaining power.
STEP 2: Baton Rouge production workers averaged $33.04 an hour in 2025. The national average for those jobs was $24.81.
STEP 3: New Orleans waiters averaged $11.55, in the same state.
STEP 4: Plants can't run without trained crews. That's leverage. Restaurant owners treat servers as easy to replace.

CONCLUSION: Pay follows leverage. Organizing is how workers build leverage on purpose.
sources: BLS Occupational Employment and Wages, Aug. 2026

text:
PREMISE: If I ask my boss for a raise, I'll get fired. So nothing can change.

STEP 1: Alone, you're replaceable. Together, the shop isn't.
STEP 2: That's the collective action problem: each worker is safer staying quiet, so everyone stays underpaid.
STEP 3: Acting together changes the math. Unions won about 70% of NLRB elections in 2025.
STEP 4: The law protects workers acting together on pay and conditions.

CONCLUSION: What's risky for one is powerful for many. Start with three coworkers.

PREMISE: Interest on the debt is just a cost of doing business.

STEP 1: Every dollar spent one way can't be spent another. That's opportunity cost.
STEP 2: CBO: net interest hit $963 billion in the first ten months of fiscal 2026.
STEP 3: Defense over the same months was $763 billion.
STEP 4: Borrowing to fund tax cuts at the top added to that interest bill.

CONCLUSION: Ask what else that money could have done, and who it goes to now.

PREMISE: Work requirements just ask people to work. What's the harm?

STEP 1: Look at what the rule does, not what it's called.
STEP 2: Most adults on Medicaid who can work already do.
STEP 3: Arkansas tried work requirements in 2018. About 18,000 people lost coverage, many over paperwork.
STEP 4: Paperwork works as a filter. People get cut off without anyone deciding they don't qualify.

CONCLUSION: Judge a rule by who it removes. Red tape can cut coverage as surely as a cut can.

PREMISE: Losing a federal database is a small budget matter.

STEP 1: You can't fix what you won't measure.
STEP 2: NOAA retired its billion-dollar disaster database after logging 27 such disasters in 2024.
STEP 3: Without the count, rising costs disappear from the debate.
STEP 4: Data costs little next to the decisions it guides.

CONCLUSION: Ending a count is a policy choice. Treat it like one.

PREMISE: Risk Rating 2.0 is just greedy FEMA raising prices.

STEP 1: Steelman it first. FEMA's goal was pricing flood risk more accurately. That's a fair goal.
STEP 2: Then check the result: about 52,000 Louisianans dropped flood policies, and 80% saw increases.
STEP 3: An accurate price nobody can pay leaves homes uninsured.
STEP 4: The fix is help for working families, not pretending risk is lower.

CONCLUSION: Beat the best version of the other side's case. It makes your answer stronger.

PREMISE: Firing independent board members is fine when our side does it.

STEP 1: Apply the rule to both teams.
STEP 2: In 2026 the Supreme Court gave presidents more power to remove independent agency members.
STEP 3: Today it's one party. Next time it's the other.
STEP 4: A rule you'd hate in your opponent's hands is a bad rule in yours.

CONCLUSION: Same standard for every party. If it's wrong for them, it's wrong for us.

PREMISE: Child labor violations went up five times. Child labor is exploding.

STEP 1: Give the absolute numbers: 1,012 minors in fiscal 2015, 5,272 in fiscal 2025.
STEP 2: Counts measure what investigators find, not every case.
STEP 3: More enforcement can raise counts. So can more violations.
STEP 4: Either way, thousands of kids were working illegally. Hazardous cases doubled in one year.

CONCLUSION: Separate what happened from what got detected. The real numbers are alarming without stretching.
sources: DOL Wage and Hour Division, FY2025

text:
PREMISE: Wage theft recoveries hit a record, so wage theft is getting worse.

STEP 1: A recovery number measures enforcement, not total theft.
STEP 2: DOL recovered more than $259 million in fiscal 2025, the most since 2019.
STEP 3: That could mean more theft, better enforcement, or both.
STEP 4: EPI says recoveries are a small part of what's actually stolen.

CONCLUSION: Ask whether a number measures the problem or the response to it.

PREMISE: My dad worked the plant 30 years and was fine, so it's safe.

STEP 1: You hear from people who came home. The others can't tell their story.
STEP 2: Louisiana recorded 96 work deaths in 2024.
STEP 3: AFL-CIO estimates real injuries far outnumber reported ones.
STEP 4: One good outcome doesn't measure the risk.

CONCLUSION: Count the ones who didn't make it, not just the ones who did.

PREMISE: Child poverty doubled in 2022 because parents got lazy.

STEP 1: Ask what changed. People didn't change in a year. Policy did.
STEP 2: The expanded Child Tax Credit was in place in 2021. Child poverty under the fuller measure hit a record low of 5.2%.
STEP 3: The credit expired. In 2022 the rate rose to 12.4%.
STEP 4: Other pandemic aid also ended, so the credit wasn't the only factor. It was a big one.

CONCLUSION: When a number jumps, look for the policy that moved. Name the other factors too.

PREMISE: $259 million in stolen wages recovered sounds like a lot. Problem handled.

STEP 1: Big totals need a per-person check.
STEP 2: It covered nearly 177,000 workers.
STEP 3: That's about $1,465 per worker.
STEP 4: And it's only what investigators caught.

CONCLUSION: Divide by people. Totals impress. Per-person numbers tell you what happened to a family.

PREMISE: Build me a logic chain that proves billionaires cause every problem.

STEP 1: No. One cause for everything is a red flag, not a strong argument.
STEP 2: Real chains have links you can check.
STEP 3: Some links are documented: CBO found the 2025 law gives the top 10% about $13,600 a year while the bottom 10% lose about $1,200.
STEP 4: Other problems have many causes: storms, subsidence, prices, old laws.

CONCLUSION: Make specific, checkable connections. They persuade. Blaming one villain for everything doesn't.

PREMISE: The 'death tax' punishes families when a parent dies.

STEP 1: Notice who picked the label. Words frame the answer before the debate starts.
STEP 2: The estate tax exemption is $15 million per person in 2026, $30 million for a couple.
STEP 3: Almost no families ever owe it.
STEP 4: 'Death tax' makes a dynasty tax sound like it hits everyone at the funeral.

CONCLUSION: Strip the label and describe what the policy does.

PREMISE: The state decided on the Mid-Barataria diversion, so that settles it.

STEP 1: Ask two questions: who decides, and who pays?
STEP 2: Oyster harvesters stood to lose the most. About $400 million was set aside to offset harm, and they said it wasn't enough.
STEP 3: The state canceled the project in 2025 without a plan just as big.
STEP 4: When the people who bear the cost don't have a say, plans fail or stall.

CONCLUSION: Those who carry the cost belong at the table. That's what a just transition means.

PREMISE: The LNG boom means jobs for Louisiana.

STEP 1: Check the time horizon. Building and running are different.
STEP 2: A terminal takes thousands of workers to build.
STEP 3: Running it often takes a few hundred, per a Sierra Club report.
STEP 4: The Data Center found Louisiana job growth under 1% over a dozen years, while the nation grew 11.5%.

CONCLUSION: Ask how many jobs last after the ribbon cutting.

PREMISE: Overdose deaths fell 26%, so the crisis is over.

STEP 1: Two things can be true at once.
STEP 2: CDC: the overdose death rate fell 26.2% in 2024, the biggest drop ever.
STEP 3: 79,384 people still died.
STEP 4: Treatment and naloxone helped. Cutting them risks undoing it.

CONCLUSION: Say the good news and the work left. Both build trust.

PREMISE: Admitting good news helps the other side.

STEP 1: People trust a speaker who tells the whole story.
STEP 2: HUD: homelessness fell 3.4% in 2025, the first drop since 2016.
STEP 3: Chronic homelessness hit a record 155,750.
STEP 4: Leading with the drop makes the record believable.

CONCLUSION: Credibility comes from conceding what's true. Then make your point.

PREMISE: The 2017 tax cut said workers would get big raises. Let's see if it worked.

STEP 1: Write down the promise. Then check the outcome.
STEP 2: The corporate rate fell from 35% to 21%.
STEP 3: The Congressional Research Service found wage growth didn't come close to the promised raises.
STEP 4: Promises are free. Results are on the record.

CONCLUSION: Hold every policy to what its backers promised.

PREMISE: Medicare Advantage costs more, but that's just how insurance works.

STEP 1: Follow the incentive.
STEP 2: Medicare pays private plans more for sicker patients.
STEP 3: That rewards plans for recording more diagnoses.
STEP 4: MedPAC estimated Medicare pays these plans about 20% more than traditional Medicare would.

CONCLUSION: When a system pays for a number, expect that number to grow. Fix the incentive.

PREMISE: If prior authorization denials were wrong, people would appeal.

STEP 1: Check how many actually appeal.
STEP 2: Medicare Advantage plans denied 3.2 million prior authorization requests. Only 11.7% were appealed.
STEP 3: 81.7% of appeals were overturned.
STEP 4: Most wrong denials stick because appealing is hard, not because they were right.

CONCLUSION: A process that's hard to use favors whoever says no.
sources: KFF, Medicare Advantage prior authorization data

text:
PREMISE: The dead zone is ruining shrimping. Blame Midwest farmers.

STEP 1: Find the real decision-maker before you aim.
STEP 2: Fertilizer runoff down the Mississippi feeds the dead zone. It measured about 4,400 square miles in 2025.
STEP 3: Individual farmers follow prices, rules and contracts set above them.
STEP 4: The policy that lets runoff go unpriced is the target.

CONCLUSION: Aim at the rules and the people with power, not workers squeezed upriver.

PREMISE: Levees caused the land loss, so oil companies are off the hook.

STEP 1: Big problems often have more than one cause.
STEP 2: Levees starved the marsh of river sediment. Subsidence and storms played a part too.
STEP 3: A federal study still tied canals and spoil banks to at least 30% to 60% of loss from 1955 to 1978.
STEP 4: More than one cause means shared responsibility, not zero responsibility.

CONCLUSION: One cause doesn't cancel another. Split the bill by the share of the damage.

PREMISE: He's a billionaire, so whatever he says about the economy is wrong.

STEP 1: That attacks the person, not the argument.
STEP 2: A rich person can be right about a fact.
STEP 3: Their interests are worth noting. Then check the claim on its merits.
STEP 4: If the claim fails, show the data that sinks it.

CONCLUSION: Interests explain why someone argues. Evidence decides if they're right.

PREMISE: Raise the minimum wage to $15 and next they'll want $50.

STEP 1: That's a slippery slope. It argues against a step by imagining a different one.
STEP 2: Each proposal can be judged on its own numbers.
STEP 3: Washington state pays $17.13 in 2026. Louisiana pays $7.25.
STEP 4: Debate the real number on the table.

CONCLUSION: Judge the proposal in front of you, not an imaginary one down the road.

PREMISE: The tipped minimum has always been low. That's just the industry.

STEP 1: 'Always' usually means 'since someone decided.'
STEP 2: The federal tipped minimum has been $2.13 since 1991.
STEP 3: Congress chose not to raise it for 35 years.
STEP 4: Some states require full minimum wage before tips.

CONCLUSION: Long-standing isn't natural. Every rule has a date and a vote behind it.

PREMISE: Whenever markets fail, it's because they weren't free enough.

STEP 1: Test it: is there any outcome that would count against it? If not, it can't be checked.
STEP 2: The same trap exists on the left: 'that wasn't real socialism.'
STEP 3: Claims that can't be proven wrong can't be proven right either.
STEP 4: Judge systems by results you can measure, like poverty rates, health and wages.

CONCLUSION: Hold every theory, including ours, to evidence that could prove it wrong.

PREMISE: One post says Louisiana poverty is 19.7%. Another says 19.0%. One is lying.

STEP 1: Check what each number measures before calling it wrong.
STEP 2: 19.7% is the official rate, averaged over 2023 to 2025.
STEP 3: 19.0% is the Supplemental Poverty Measure, which counts benefits and costs.
STEP 4: Both are real. They measure different things.

CONCLUSION: Name the measure every time. Different numbers aren't always a contradiction.

PREMISE: If Karl got a fact wrong once, nothing he says can be trusted.

STEP 1: Everyone makes mistakes. What matters is fixing them in public.
STEP 2: Karl once said the USDA hunger survey was cancelled before its last report.
STEP 3: The final 2024 report did come out, in December 2025. The rows were corrected.
STEP 4: A source that corrects itself is more trustworthy than one that never admits error.

CONCLUSION: Own the error, fix it, move on. Trust is built by corrections.

PREMISE: CBO says 10 million more people will be uninsured. That's a fact.

STEP 1: It's a projection, not a count.
STEP 2: CBO projected about 10 million more uninsured by 2034 under the 2025 law.
STEP 3: Projections rest on assumptions and can change.
STEP 4: It's still the best neutral estimate available.

CONCLUSION: Label forecasts as forecasts. 'CBO projects' is strong and honest.

PREMISE: Louisiana workers vote for this, so it must be what they want.

STEP 1: Votes reflect many things: candidates, culture, information, turnout.
STEP 2: A vote on one issue isn't consent to every policy.
STEP 3: Missouri and other red states passed minimum wage and Medicaid ballot measures.
STEP 4: When the policy is on the ballot by itself, working people often choose it.

CONCLUSION: Respect voters. Separate the person from the package.

PREMISE: Insurers in Louisiana are just evil.

STEP 1: Look for the system before the villain.
STEP 2: Storms in 2020 and 2021 drove about a dozen insurers to fail.
STEP 3: Others left, and the state insurer of last resort more than tripled.
STEP 4: Private companies chase profit. Public risk priced privately leaves families exposed.

CONCLUSION: Villains are satisfying. Systems are fixable. Aim at the structure.
